text: Last lesson's canary rollout paused at each traffic weight, but a pause on its own isn't a decision — nothing in that YAML actually checked whether it was safe to move forward. This lesson closes that gap: automatically gating the rollout on real metrics instead of a fixed timer.

In practice, that advance-or-abort call either falls to a human watching a Grafana dashboard in real time, which falls apart the moment you're shipping more than a handful of deployments a day, or it just doesn't happen, and the rollout marches forward on a clock regardless of what's actually going on. Progressive delivery wires that decision directly into the metrics themselves.

Argo Rollouts does this with an AnalysisTemplate — a resource that defines a query and a pass-fail threshold, run automatically at each canary step. This is the exact same Prometheus and PromQL from the observability course, now driving a deployment decision instead of a dashboard panel. This query computes the ratio of 5xx responses to total requests over a five-minute window; successCondition says that has to stay at or below 1 percent, and failureLimit 2 means it takes two consecutive failed checks, not one blip, to call it a real failure.

The Rollout references that template directly inside its canary steps. Now every setWeight is followed by an actual check against live production metrics. If error rate at 10 percent weight stays under the threshold, it proceeds to 50 automatically. If it breaches the threshold, Argo Rollouts aborts on its own and shifts traffic back to the previous stable version — nobody has to notice a dashboard or page anyone first.

Error rate is the most common signal, but a realistic setup usually watches latency too — a version that's technically correct but noticeably slower is still a regression worth catching. And the threshold matters as much as the metric itself: too strict, and ordinary variance triggers false rollbacks; too loose, and a real regression sails through.

What this still can't catch is a bug that only shows up once a feature is actually released to users, not just deployed to a small slice of traffic — and that's exactly the distinction feature flags are built to handle, coming up next.
